Councilman Clendenin, City Council, and to the Tampa community that is here in council and those watching from home, I am very proud to be standing before you to present the City Of Tampa's FY 2026 budget. This year's theme: grounded in progress reflects the priorities we've heard loud and clear from residents across Tampa in town halls, neighborhood meetings, and more than a few grocery store conversations. You've told us what matters most. This budget is built around those values: resilience, responsibility, efficiency, and results. Tampa has become one of the most exciting cities in the country, but great cities aren't built on buzz; they are built on strong foundations -- roads, stormwater systems, and water lines may not be glamorous, but they keep our city running. When we invest in the basics, we unlock opportunity, strengthen resilience, and lay the foundation for future growth. And we're stretching every dollar to work harder and smarter. Cities are often criticized for adding new positions to their workforce, but this morning, you're going to hear about how the employees we've added over the past few years, including over a hundred firefighters, 60 police officers, in-house paving and water repair teams, and our in-house waste-to-energy team have either made our city safer or have saved taxpayers millions of dollars. A great example of how hiring an energy manager has saved us over $1.4 Million in energy costs. This budget is our blueprint, a plan to deliver core services, modernize infrastructure, and invest in Tampa's future. We're doing it in a way that ensures we maintain our near-perfect credit rating. Tampa has the second highest municipal bond rating in the nation, which, as you know, saves our taxpayers millions of dollars every year. Tampa is one of the safest cities our size in the nation, and that is no accident. It's the result of strategic investment and a relentless focus on public safety. That's why every single dollar of property tax revenue in the proposed 2026 budget is spent on Tampa Police and Fire. And it'S Been That Way for years. In 2026, we're bringing in 380 million in property tax revenue, and we're spending 455 million on police and fire for public safety. It's a clear reflection of our priorities, protecting lives, property, and peace of mind. This is a message that we want the entire community to share with their legislators in tallahassee. Property taxes fund public safety. In Tampa, we support our First Responders, and we couldn't do it without this funding. When hurricane helene and milton hit, our First Responders answered over 15,000 emergency calls and rescued hundreds of residents from rising floodwaters. But it's the day-to-day work they do that keeps our city strong. Crime is down over 20%. Violent crime is down 19%, and homicides are down 63% this year alone. Initiatives like the police athletic league, our rich houses and community violence intervention program are making neighborhoods safer, not just today, but for years to come. They are making them safer for the youth in our community who are the future. Tampa Fire Rescue responded to over 92,000 calls last year. Many of them lifesaving medical emergencies. That's why we've prioritized the tools and infrastructure that they need, from adding additional rescue units, a pump truck, new equipment, and technology as well as over a hundred additional firefighters. Public safety isn't just a budget line item, it is the backbone of our community. For most Tampa residents, life after the hurricane looks normal again, but for too many of our neighbors, especially those who lost everything, the devastation still lingers. Storms may pass quickly, but their impact lasts. I saw it firsthand, helping families haul out soaked furniture and salvage what they could from homes flooded by helene and milton. I understand the very real fear that it could happen again. That's why this budget puts a sharp focus on resilience. We can't build -- outbuild nature, but we can prepare. We've launched a pump station rapid response team and we're installing temporary generators at stormwater pumps in our most vulnerable neighborhoods. This budget invests $11 billion toward permanent backup generators that will be installed over the next two years. Stormwater crews are working SIX days a week clearing debris, keeping systems moving, and delivering on the basics that matter the most during storms. Just in the past year alone, we've removed 6,800 tons of debris from our drains and ditches and Our Street Sweeping Team has prevented another 5,580 tons from entering the system to begin with. Combined, that's over 12,000 tons of yard waste, landscaping, and other debris. We've already invested 350 million in major flood relief projects, including macdill 48 nature park which serves both as flood protection and community greenspace. We finished major projects in Seminole Heights and in South Tampa. These projects have made a difference all across our city, and that's why we're excited to move forward with those projects that are in the pipeline. Since launching the pipes program, we've replaced over 62 miles of aging waterlines and 200 miles of wastewater pipe. Many of these pipes were over a hundred years old. And in 2026 we'll invest another 79 million into replacing this crumbling, yet critical infrastructure that's essential to our well-being. We're also leading the nation with the first suspended ion exchange system to remove pfas and other chemicals from our drinking water, improving safety while cutting treatment costs. And thanks to the efficiency of our in-house water repair crews, we've saved Tampa taxpayers over $15 million by fixing main breaks ourselves instead of turning those jobs over to contractors. As you know, Tampa is a city on the move. And we're meeting our transportation challenges with smart, efficient solutions despite the huge blow of losing the surtax dollars supported overwhelmingly by Tampa voters. We resurfaced over 235 miles of streets since 2019 and by investing in two in-house paving teams, we've been able to double our paving capacity at half the price and complete the jobs in half the time. And we are not stopping. Thanks to these teams, we also repaired more feet of sidewalk in the past year than the city has done in the past decade. Our resurfacing team's work will continue into this fiscal year. In 2026, we'll continue to build out our walk-bike network. We already added 56 miles of bike lanes and this budget will expand the green spine, complete the first two phases of the green artery and connect neighborhoods like never before. These two projects alone will connect West Tampa to East Tampa and neighborhoods like Seminole Heights, Sulphur Springs and East Tampa to our downtown. The new west riverwalk will be more than a scenic path and mobility corridor. It is the hub of our citywide walk-bike network connecting Tampa's neighborhoods together and residents to jobs, education, and shopping. It's also an amenity that will serve as an economic catalyst for West Tampa that ensures public access to the riverfront for generations to come. This budget also helps Restore Downtown Street grid to improve connections and reduce congestion. It takes concrete steps toward the start of construction on the future streetcar extension by moving forward with Planning and development for both project and funding operations. Thanks to our participation in the U.s. Department of Transportation's regional infrastructure accelerate, which launches next month, we're starting to see viable conversation about our region's transportation future, and that includes big projects like the airport to downtown connection. And you may have heard that Bright Line plans to issue 400 million in bonds to fund part of the orlando to Tampa extension. We're excited about this Bright Line extension. It will finally make it easy for disney fans to visit Tampa Bay where the magic includes stanley cups, super bowls, baseball and sunsets that don't require an admission fee. The work is happening. The network is forming, and the vision is coming into focus. With over 200 parks, we're raising the standard for public space citywide. Of course, the crown jewel is fair oaks recreation complex, a 10-acre state-of-the-art campus in East Tampa that reflects what happens when the community leads on design. It will feature a senior center, Basketball Court, pickleball courts, classrooms, weight rooms and so much more. It is nearly complete, and it will be a game-changer. Maintaining our parks across the city is just as important. We're providing additional general fund dollars for basic upgrades and improvements at neighborhood facilities. As we all know, housing continues to be a challenge nationwide, but this City Council and administration have remained steadfast about working to prevent our family, friends, and neighbors from being priced out of Tampa. Home prices surged, and we acted. Since 2020, we've added 20,000 residential units, including thousands of affordable homes. We used every tool available, from zoning reform to down payment assistance, and we kept construction moving while others paused. Now rental rates have returned to the 2021 levels. That's progress, but we definitely are not done. This fiscal year we processed nearly 23,000 permits representing almost $2.5 Billion in development. The army navy development will create hundreds of affordable and market rate units and transform a surface parking lot into a beautiful downtown gateway. Smart growth is at the forefront of our new comprehensive plan and with City Council's leadership, we'll add density where it makes sense along commercial and transit corridors while protecting the character and the historic neighborhoods that make Tampa unique. It's also about breaking down silos. The type of development that we need to grow in a way that preserves our quality of life depends on what our future transportation system looks like. We've built new neighborhoods. We've modernized infrastructure. We've opened new parks, created housing, and made our streets safer and more connected. Our streetcar is on track for 1.4 Million riders this year. Our rainy day fund is strong. Our bond rating is among the best in the nation. And for the first time, Tampa's median household income surpasses $70,000. Time Magazine says Tampa is one of the world's best places. Forbes calls Tampa the Best Place to live in Florida. And the financial times ranks us the top u.s. City for international business. But our greatest asset is not a headline. It's our people. It's in how we show up for each other when things get hard. It's in how we work together to get things done, and it's how we move forward united and grounded in progress. Now, i'm pleased to bring up our chief financial officer Dennis Rogero. segments.text: Yes, mr. Chairman, good morning. Good morning members of the public, Martin Shelby, City Council attorney, here to talk to you briefly about the rules for public comment and the decorum for today's meeting. With regard to public comment, you've had the opportunity to submit cards outside for general public comment and one card per speaker. Each person submitting a card will be recognized by name to approach and speak. A three-minute time limit applies and please print legibly because names that cannot be read will not be called. If you are here to speak on something on the agenda that's been designated as a public hearing, you will have time to speak to that item at the time of the public hearing and use the sign-in sheet that's outside instead of the public speaker card. If you need assistance, please see the City Staff. Members of the public are allowed a reasonable opportunity at the beginning of today's agenda to address any item on the agenda before the City Council takes official action on an item. Again, if it's something set for staff reports or something on the consent docket, the time to speak to that is now. A three minute time limit applies, as I said. Members of the public are also reminded to please refrain from disruptive behavior, including making vulgar or threatening remarks or making or causing disruptive noises or sounds or displaying signs or graphics. Speakers are also reminded to refrain from launching personal attacks against any city official, staff member, or members of the public. The Chair Will rule out of order any person who speaks without being recognized or attempts to address the council from outside the speaker area at the podium. Persons failing to comply with the council rules may also be ruled out of order and at the discretion of the Chair may be removed from the chambers for the remainder of today's meeting. Now, finally, please note that City Council should refrain from engaging a speaker under public comment. And the public should be aware that City Council does not take questions or have a dialogue with you during agenda public comment. This is your opportunity to express your position. Thank you.

Exercised our right to peacefully protest and we were met with violence as one activist knocked to the ground bleeding.
